subject: Transect Placement in Complex Study Area

messages.author: 0d2a4151de2c5ae2
messages.subject: Transect Placement in Complex Study Area
parts:
Hi all,

I am designing a survey on a large and complex lake with many islands and bays. I have attached a map of the area. What is the best approach for choosing line transects in study areas that have many obstacles?

The area will be surveyed by boat and I want to minimize interruptions of transects that will require the crew to drive around a large island or peninsula to finish surveying the other side of the transect. Fuel and time are expensive!

I have thought about generating a ton of segmented line transects at all different angles and then systematically weeding out the ones that have poor navigability and then choosing a random subset of the remaining transects. But I imagine there is a better method...

Thank you!

Simone

messages.author: 875f0a74e1b42050
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Transect Placement in Complex Study Area
parts:
Dear Simone,

I  wonder if there is any possibility of using an aircraft? I suspect a good survey design for a boat based distance sampling survey might end up being fairly expensive.

However, another important consideration is whether distance sampling is an appropriate method to use in this area as it is fairly small. Do you know how many detections you might expect to get? If you don't have pilot survey data you could try some basic simulations to get an idea based on your expectations of the population. 

If you planned to proceed with a boat based survey the method you suggest of weeding out the transects which give poor navigability sounds like it will lead to a non-uniform coverage design. The more complicated the area the less likely it is to be surveyed and if density of animals in these areas differs to the rest of the region then conventional distance sampling estimates will be biased. 

I wondered about whether some parts of your region might be suitable for census counts and in other areas cluster sampling might help a bit. Have a look at this paper: https://journal.iwc.int/index.php/jcrm/article/view/687/412
I'm unsure of how much effort you have available for the study. 

Kind regards,
Laura
